records.title: Quine Architecture: Native POSIX Process Mapping for Agent Substrates
records.relevance_note: Details the transition from user-space application middleware to kernel-level agent tracking via process IDs and system calls.
records.reason_included: Provides a high-value, specific mechanism (execve) for overcoming context saturation without losing process identity.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Agent instances map directly to a Process ID, passing the overarching mission via the immutable argument vector array and routing diagnostics to standard error to prevent deliverable pollution.
Solves context window exhaustion by externalizing progress markers into environment variables and invoking the execve system call to flush saturated memory while retaining computational identity.

Section 'Realizing Agents as Native POSIX Processes', Paragraph 4

records.title: Stateless Execution and Lightweight Namespace Sandboxing
records.relevance_note: Evaluates containerless process isolation techniques optimized for high-throughput evaluation and linear trajectory logging.
records.reason_included: Contains measured improvements in storage and cold-start latency by bypassing heavy container virtualization.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Bypasses heavy containers entirely by relying on Linux namespaces, root directory changes, and bind mounts to create secure, container-free isolated environments.
Reduces storage requirements to 5% of comparable containerized baselines and shortens environment preparation time to 25% while maintaining strict process isolation.

records.title: Immutable Micro-Virtualization and Git-Like Branching in Execution Substrates
records.relevance_note: Explores substrates utilizing microVM snapshotting to enable non-linear, tree-based exploration and hypothesis testing.
records.reason_included: Critical architectural pattern for achieving cheap branching and guaranteed recovery from destructive exploratory actions.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Agents establish branch points by explicitly setting a persistence flag during command execution; the runtime captures differential changes to produce a cryptographically unique filesystem state.
The immutability of the root image combined with copy-on-write differencing allows the runtime to instantly roll back corrupted filesystems without resource penalty.

records.title: Kernel-Level Resource Governance for Agentic Workloads via eBPF
records.relevance_note: A foundational empirical study on the resource consumption dynamics of agents compared to traditional microservices.
records.reason_included: Identifies the 15.4x peak-to-average memory ratio of agent tool calls and provides the eBPF dynamic boundary mitigation mechanism.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Tool-driven bursts generate a peak-to-average memory ratio exceeding 15.4x, with memory utilization fluctuating by up to 3GB within a single one-second interval.

Intent-driven resource controllers implemented via extended Berkeley Packet Filters (eBPF) enforce dynamic memory limits at the exact boundary of the tool call, reducing allocation latency by nearly 30%.

Section 'Intent-Driven Control via Extended Packet Filters', Paragraph 2 & 3

records.title: Standardization and Governance via the Model Context Protocol
records.relevance_note: Focuses on the security and governance aspects of utilizing the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a universal execution substrate.
records.reason_included: Extracts the mechanism by which adapter API traffic is correlated with kernel events to verify model intent against execution reality.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Modern substrate deployments enforce strict governance by classifying adapter servers as resource guardians that utilize proof keys for code exchange and resource indicators.
Advanced substrates intercept API traffic and correlate it with kernel events monitored via packet filters to ensure the reasoning trace matches executed system calls.
